input: SELECT customer_id, order_id, order_date, julianday(order_date) - julianday(LAG(order_date) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date)) AS gap_days FROM orders;

input: WITH pr AS (SELECT p.product_id, p.name, p.category_id, SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS rev FROM products p JOIN order_items oi ON oi.product_id = p.product_id GROUP BY p.product_id) SELECT name, ROUND(100.0 * rev / SUM(rev) OVER (PARTITION BY category_id), 1) AS pct_of_category FROM pr;

input: SELECT p.name, COUNT(DISTINCT c.country) AS n_countries FROM products p JOIN order_items oi ON oi.product_id = p.product_id JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = oi.order_id JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id GROUP BY p.product_id HAVING n_countries >= 3 ORDER BY n_countries DESC;

input: SELECT c.country, cat.name, ROUND(SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price), 2) AS rev FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id JOIN products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id JOIN categories cat ON cat.category_id = p.category_id GROUP BY c.country, cat.name HAVING rev > 200 ORDER BY rev DESC;

  - rev: the total revenue for that country and category, calculated as the sum over all matching order items of (quantity × unit_price), rounded to 2 decimals
- Which rows are included (the joins and grouping explain this):
  - It starts from customers who have placed orders (inner join from customers to orders), then to the items in those orders (order_items), then to the products for those items, and finally to the category of each product. So only country/category combinations that actually occurred in orders are included. Customers with no orders don’t contribute, and orders with no items don’t either.
  - It groups results by country and category, so you get one row per country/category pair.
- Filter applied: only rows with rev > 200 are kept (i.e., country/category pairs whose total revenue exceeds 200).
- Ordering: the results are sorted by rev in descending order (highest revenue first). If two rows have the same rev, the query does not specify a secondary sort, so their relative order is not defined by the query.
- What is explicitly not filtered: there is no restriction by order status in the query, so all orders whatever their status (completed, pending, cancelled) are counted in the revenue.
- In short: the query tells you, for each country and product category, how much revenue has been earned from orders in that country for products in that category, considering all orders and statuses, and only shows the country/category pairs that earned more than 200 in total, with the largest earnings shown first.

It is clear and makes no unsupported claims.

input: WITH t AS (SELECT o.customer_id, SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS spent FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id WHERE o.status = 'completed' GROUP BY o.customer_id) SELECT c.name, ROUND(t.spent, 2) FROM t JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = t.customer_id WHERE t.spent > (SELECT AVG(spent) FROM t) ORDER BY t.spent DESC;
output:
- What it returns in plain words: the list of customers who have spent more than the average amount, but only considering their completed orders. For each of those customers, it shows the customer’s name and the total amount they spent (rounded to 2 decimals).
- How the rows are created:
  1) The CTE t gathers, for every customer who has at least one completed order, the total money spent on those completed orders. It sums, for each customer, quantity times unit price across all their completed orders.
  2) The main query keeps only those customers whose total spent is greater than the average total spent across all customers in t. This means customers who spent above the overall average from that completed-orders dataset.
  3) It joins back to the customers table to obtain the customer name.
- How the row order is determined: the result is sorted by spent from highest to lowest (DESC), so the customer who spent the most appears first.
- What is not included: customers who have no completed orders are not included, since the CTE only creates rows for customers with completed orders. Also, orders with status other than 'completed' are ignored.
- Summary: you get the names of the customers who spent more than the average on completed orders, along with their total spent (rounded to two decimals), ordered from highest spender to lowest.
reason: The explanation correctly and completely describes the query: the CTE sums quantity * unit_price per customer for orders with status = 'completed', the main query keeps customers whose summed spent is strictly greater than the average of those sums, joins to customers to return the name and the spent (rounded to 2 decimals), and orders results by spent descending. It also notes exclusion of customers without completed orders.

input: SELECT c.name, COUNT(DISTINCT substr(o.order_date, 1, 7)) AS active_months FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id GROUP BY c.customer_id HAVING active_months >= 6 ORDER BY active_months DESC;

- The query uses an inner join between customers and orders, so only customers who have at least one order are included. Customers with no orders are excluded.
- For each included customer, it counts how many distinct year-month values appear in their orders. It does this by taking the first seven characters of order_date (YYYY-MM) and counting distinct values, which is the number of active months the customer placed orders in.
- The result includes one row per customer (GROUP BY customer_id), showing the customer’s name and the count of distinct active months as active_months.
- The HAVING clause keeps only customers whose active_months is at least 6, i.e., customers who placed orders in at least six different months.
- The rows are ordered by active_months in descending order (highest number of active months first).
- No filter on order status is applied, so all orders (whatever their status) are counted.
reason: The explanation accurately and completely describes the join, the distinct year-month counting via the first seven characters of order_date, the grouping by customer, the HAVING filter (>=6 months), and the descending ordering; it makes no unsupported claims and is written in plain terms a non-SQL reader can follow.

input: WITH ot AS (SELECT o.customer_id, o.order_id, o.order_date, SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS total FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id GROUP BY o.order_id) SELECT customer_id, order_id, ROUND(AVG(total) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS moving_avg FROM ot;
output:
This query reports, for every order that actually has line items, a short moving-average measure of that customer’s spending on recent orders.

What’s in the intermediate step (the WITH ot AS ...):
- It takes each order and adds up (quantity × unit_price) for all items in that order. This gives total spend for that order.
- It only includes orders that have at least one order item (because it joins orders to order_items).
- Each resulting row contains: customer_id, order_id, order_date, and total (the money spent on that order).

What the outer query does:
- For every row from the intermediate result, it computes a moving average of total spending across the same customer’s orders, in date order, using the current order and the two immediately earlier orders (a 3-order window). In plain terms: for each order, look at that customer’s most recent up to 3 orders (ending with this one) and average their order totals.
- The moving average is rounded to 2 decimal places and returns as moving_avg.

Row inclusion and order specifics:
- Rows covered: every order that has at least one item (i.e., orders that appear in order_items).
- Left-out rows: any order with no line items is excluded (because there’s no corresponding order_item data to sum).
- Partitioning and ordering: the moving-average is computed separately for each customer (partition by customer_id) and ordered by order_date within that customer.
- Window behavior when a customer has fewer than 3 orders: the average uses however many orders exist so far (1 to 3), not a fixed 3; there is no filtering to require a minimum window.

input: WITH RECURSIVE months(m) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT m + 1 FROM months WHERE m < 12) SELECT m, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE CAST(strftime('%m', order_date) AS INTEGER) = m) AS n_orders FROM months;
output: This query builds a list of the numbers 1 through 12 (one row per month, January=1, February=2, …, December=12) using a recursive common table expression. For each month m in that list, it then counts how many orders have an order_date whose month part equals m. The count includes all orders, regardless of their status or year. So the result has 12 rows: for month 1 to 12, the second column is the total number of orders placed in that calendar month (across all years). If a month has no orders in the data, the count will be 0. The rows appear in increasing month order: 1, 2, ..., 12. There is no sorting beyond that.

input: SELECT AVG(price) FROM (SELECT price FROM products ORDER BY price LIMIT 2 - (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM products) % 2 OFFSET ((SELECT COUNT(*) FROM products) - 1) / 2);
output:
This query calculates the median price of all products in the products table. It does this by:
- considering every product’s price and sorting them from cheapest to most expensive,
- if there is an even number of products, taking the two middle prices and averaging them; if there is an odd number, taking just the single middle price,
- then returning that value as AVG(price) (which becomes the median when applied to the one or two middle prices).

In short: it returns one number—the median price of all products (for an even count, the average of the two middle prices; for an odd count, the middle price itself).
reason: The explanation correctly and clearly states that the query sorts product prices ascending, selects either the single middle price (odd count) or the two middle prices (even count), and returns their average as the median. It mentions the ordering direction and the even/odd selection logic and makes no unsupported claims.

input: SELECT o.order_date, SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS rev FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id GROUP BY o.order_date ORDER BY rev DESC LIMIT 1;
output:
This query finds the single date (order_date) on which the company earned the most revenue, based on items sold on orders with actual line items.

- It combines orders with their line items using an inner join on order_id, so only orders that have at least one item are considered.
- For each order_date, it sums quantity times unit_price across all items on all orders of that date. This sum is labeled rev and represents total revenue for that date (for all orders that date, whatever their order status).
- It groups results by order_date, so you get one row per date with the revenue for that date.
- It sorts the dates by rev in descending order and returns only the top row due to LIMIT 1. If multiple dates tie for the highest revenue, only one of them is returned.

In short: the query returns one row containing the date with the highest total revenue and that revenue amount for that date, considering all orders with at least one item and regardless of order status.
reason: The explanation accurately and completely describes the query: it notes the inner join (so only orders with items), the SUM of quantity * unit_price grouped by order_date, the descending ORDER BY on rev and LIMIT 1, and that all order statuses are included. The language is clear to a non-SQL reader and does not claim anything the SQL does not do.

input: WITH q AS (SELECT o.customer_id, (CAST(strftime('%m', o.order_date) AS INTEGER) + 2) / 3 AS qtr, SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS rev FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id GROUP BY o.customer_id, qtr), d AS (SELECT customer_id, rev - LAG(rev) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY qtr) AS delta FROM q) SELECT customer_id FROM d GROUP BY customer_id HAVING MIN(COALESCE(delta, 0)) >= 0;

WITH u AS (SELECT product_id, SUM(quantity) AS units FROM order_items GROUP BY product_id) SELECT p.name, u.units FROM u JOIN products p ON p.product_id = u.product_id WHERE u.units > (SELECT AVG(units) FROM u) ORDER BY u.units DESC;
output:
This query finds which products sold more units than the average number of units sold per product. It does this by first computing, for every product, the total quantity sold across all orders (the units column). It then keeps only those products whose total units is greater than the average of all those per-product totals. For each of those products, it shows the product name and the total units sold.

Notes:
- The results include only products that have at least one sold unit (they appear because they have an entry in order_items).
- The final list is ordered from greatest total units sold to smallest (highest totals first).
- There is no filter on order status or date in this query; it considers all orders and all statuses because those details aren’t restricted here.
reason: The explanation correctly and completely describes the query: it sums quantities per product only for products appearing in order_items, computes the average over those per-product totals, keeps products with totals greater than that average, returns the product name and total units, and orders results by units descending. It also correctly notes there is no filtering by order status or date.
